reviewNote: Teaching points and plans follow standard references: the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) scale, the International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, third edition (ICROP3), the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) study, and the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) Preferred Practice Patterns. They are for learning, not patient care. Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) stage descriptions follow the ROP-VL dataset (Creative Commons, CC BY 4.0).

tracks.title: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) reading
tracks.modality: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (OCT), macular B-scan (cross-section)

NO: Foveal pit with a smooth, symmetric contour
Every layer continuous, including the ellipsoid zone
No intraretinal or subretinal fluid. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) line smooth
AMD: Drusen (yellow deposits): dome-shaped elevations of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)
Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (AMD, wet AMD): subretinal fluid, pigment epithelial detachment, subretinal hyperreflective (bright) material
Atrophic (dry) AMD: RPE loss with light passing into the choroid (hypertransmission)
DME: Hyporeflective (dark) cystoid spaces within the retina
Hyperreflective foci (bright dots) and exudates. Subretinal fluid in some eyes
ERM: Hyperreflective (bright) band on the inner retinal surface
Wrinkled inner retina and a flattened or lost foveal pit
Diffuse thickening. Traction cysts in some eyes
RVO: Cystoid macular edema with inner retinal thickening
Branch occlusion: often sectoral, respecting the horizontal raphe (the midline the vessels do not cross)
Look for disorganised inner layers and hyperreflective foci
RAO: Acute: thickened, hyperreflective inner retina with shadowing of the outer layers (the inner retina, fed by the central retinal artery, is swollen)
Chronic: thinning and atrophy of the inner retina
Outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) are relatively preserved
VID: Macular hole: full-thickness foveal defect, often with cystic edges
Lamellar hole: partial-thickness defect with an irregular foveal contour
Vitreomacular traction: vitreous still attached at the fovea, distorting it

tracks.pearl: Read an optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan outside in. Vitreous and interface, inner retina, fluid spaces, outer retina and ellipsoid zone. Then the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), then the choroid.

foundation.label: Fluid in the retina (diabetic macular edema or vein occlusion)

plan.AMD: Separate wet from dry. Fluid or subretinal material means urgent retina referral for anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections (ranibizumab, aflibercept or bevacizumab). Drusen alone means monitoring. Give Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 (AREDS2) supplements for intermediate age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
plan.DME: Refer to retina. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections (ranibizumab, aflibercept or bevacizumab) are first line for centre-involving diabetic macular edema (DME) with reduced vision. Optimise glucose, blood pressure and lipids.
plan.ERM: Observe while vision is good. Pars plana vitrectomy with epiretinal membrane peel if distortion or vision loss affects daily life.
plan.RVO: Treat macular edema with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections. Watch for neovascularisation (new vessels). Manage systemic risk: blood pressure, diabetes, lipids.
plan.RAO: An acute retinal artery occlusion is an eye stroke. Refer the same day on the stroke pathway. If over 50, check erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) for giant cell arteritis.
plan.VID: Full-thickness macular hole: vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane (ILM) peel. Lamellar hole or traction: observe, operate if it progresses or vision falls.

tracks.title: Optic disc
tracks.modality: Fundus photograph cropped to the optic disc

normal: Pink neuroretinal rim that follows the ISNT pattern (rim thickest inferior, then superior, nasal, temporal)
Cup size in proportion to disc size: a large disc can have a large cup
glaucoma: Enlarged vertical cup, or rim thinning that breaks the ISNT pattern (inferior, superior, nasal, temporal rim order)
Focal notching, most often inferotemporal or superotemporal
Disc haemorrhage at the rim, bayoneting vessels (sharp kinks at the rim), beta-zone peripapillary atrophy

tracks.pearl: Judge the rim, not the cup-to-disc ratio alone. Always estimate disc size first.

plan.normal: Routine review. A large cup in a large disc can be normal.
plan.glaucoma: Confirm and stage: intraocular pressure (IOP), gonioscopy, visual fields and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the nerve fibre layer. Treat to a target pressure.

tracks.title: Diabetic retinopathy
tracks.sub: Grade 0 to 4 (International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy, ICDR, scale)

0: No microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates or new vessels
1: Microaneurysms only: tiny, sharp red dots
2: More than microaneurysms but less than severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)
Dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots
3: 4-2-1 rule, any one of these. More than 20 haemorrhages in each of 4 quadrants. Venous beading in 2 or more quadrants. Prominent intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) in 1 or more quadrant
4: New vessels on the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE)

tracks.pearl: One macula-centred photograph cannot show all four quadrants. So severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) is a judgement from what is visible. Grade the worst lesion you can see.

plan.1: Rescreen in 12 months. Optimise glucose, blood pressure and lipids.
plan.2: Refer to ophthalmology. Review in 6 to 12 months without macular oedema, 3 to 6 months with non-central oedema. Centre-involving oedema needs treatment (American Academy of Ophthalmology, AAO, Diabetic Retinopathy Preferred Practice Pattern 2024).
plan.3: Urgent ophthalmology referral. Panretinal laser is often considered, especially if follow-up is uncertain.
plan.4: Urgent treatment: panretinal laser and/or anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections. Vitrectomy for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage.

tracks.title: Retinopathy of prematurity
tracks.sub: Stage, aggressive retinopathy of prematurity (A-ROP) or treated

normal: No retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) signs. The peripheral retina may still be incompletely vascularised (vessels not yet grown to the edge)
s1: Demarcation line: a thin, flat white line between vascular and avascular retina
s2: Ridge: the line gains height and width, white to pink
Small isolated neovascular tufts may sit behind it
s3: Extraretinal neovascular proliferation from the ridge into the vitreous
Ragged posterior edge of the ridge
s4: Partial retinal detachment: 4A spares the fovea, 4B involves it
s5: Total retinal detachment. International Classification of ROP, third edition (ICROP3): 5A open funnel, 5B closed funnel, 5C with anterior segment changes
arop: Rapid, severe disease with marked plus disease (dilated, twisted posterior vessels)
Flat, often subtle neovascularisation (new vessels) at the vascular-avascular border, typically posterior
May skip the classic stage sequence
laser: White or pigmented laser spots in the peripheral avascular retina

tracks.descSource: ROP-VL disease descriptions (Creative Commons, CC BY 4.0), paraphrased
tracks.pearl: Treat Type 1 retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), as defined by the Early Treatment for ROP (ETROP) study. Zone I any stage with plus. Zone I stage 3 without plus. Zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus.

foundation.label: Active retinopathy of prematurity (stage 1 to 3, or aggressive ROP)

plan.normal: Continue screening until the retina is fully vascularised.
plan.s1: Review in 1 to 2 weeks. Zone and plus disease, not stage alone, decide treatment.
plan.s2: Review in 1 to 2 weeks. Treat if it meets Type 1 (zone I with plus, or zone II with plus).
plan.s3: Treat if Type 1 (zone I stage 3, or zone II stage 3 with plus). Otherwise review within a week.
plan.s5: Refer for vitreoretinal surgery. Visual prognosis is poor.
plan.arop: Treat urgently with laser or anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injection, such as ranibizumab or bevacizumab. Do not wait for the classic stages.
plan.laser: Follow up for regression and late problems: myopia (short sight), strabismus (squint), amblyopia (lazy eye), retinal detachment.

tracks.title: Image cases
tracks.modality: Slit lamp, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), fundus photo, optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), ocular ultrasound

tracks.title: General retina screening

normal: Clear media, sharp disc and vessels, no labelled disease sign on this photo
CME: Multiple cyst-like fluid pockets in the macula, often in a petaloid (flower-petal) pattern
Retina looks thickened at the fovea; central vision is blurred
Common after cataract surgery, uveitis, diabetic macular edema or a vein occlusion
CRS: Yellow-white patch of active retinochoroidal inflammation (inflamed retina and choroid), sometimes beside an old pigmented scar
Overlying vitreous haze or cells when the lesion is active
Common causes: toxoplasmosis, tuberculosis, viral retinitis
CSR: Shallow, dome-shaped serous (clear fluid) detachment of the neurosensory retina at the macula
Round or oval area of subretinal fluid with a sharp edge
Typically a young or middle-aged adult, often stressed or on steroids
EDN: Yellow-white lipid deposits with sharp, waxy edges
Often ringed around a leaking vessel or microaneurysm (a circinate, ring-shaped, pattern)
A sign of chronic vascular leakage, most often diabetic or hypertensive
MH: Reduced clarity of the fundus view from a hazy media rather than a retinal lesion
Vessels and disc look blurred or veiled, not sharply focused
Causes: cataract, vitreous haemorrhage, or inflammation of the media
MS: Well-defined pale or pigmented flat lesion at the macula. Causes: healed inflammation, trauma or neovascularisation (new vessels)
Vision loss is fixed and usually central
MYA: Pale, tessellated (tiled-looking) fundus with visible large choroidal vessels
Peripapillary crescent beside a tilted or stretched disc
High myopia can add a posterior staphyloma (outpouching of the back of the eye), lacquer cracks or myopic choroidal neovascularisation
ODC: Enlarged cup relative to the disc, with rim thinning that can break the ISNT pattern (inferior, superior, nasal, temporal rim order)
May show a notch or a disc haemorrhage in progressive cases
The chief fundus-photo red flag for glaucoma
RD: Retina lifted off the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). It looks pale, out of focus and folded, with darker vessels than the surrounding retina
Wavy or corrugated surface, sometimes with a visible break
Sight- and eye-threatening; needs urgent referral
RT: Retina pulled into peaks or straight folds by fibrovascular or membranous tissue
Vessels are dragged or distorted along the line of traction
Seen in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, after trauma, or with vitreomacular traction
TD: Oval, obliquely inserted optic disc. An inferior or inferonasal crescent of exposed sclera or choroid
Often paired with myopia, on a fundus that looks stretched inferiorly
A benign congenital variant that can mimic a field defect, not glaucoma itself

tracks.pearl: Each Retinal Fundus Multi-disease Image Dataset (RFMiD) photo here carries one label. Real fundi often show more than one of these signs together. So keep scanning the whole photo even after you spot the first one.

plan.CME: Treat the cause. After surgery: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or steroid drops. Vascular causes: anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) or steroid. Refer to retina if it persists.
plan.CRS: Identify the organism where possible (serology, polymerase chain reaction, PCR). Treat the specific infection first. Add an oral steroid only under antimicrobial cover.
plan.CSR: Most resolve spontaneously in 1 to 3 months. Stop steroids if possible and observe. Photodynamic therapy (verteporfin) or a leak-directed laser for chronic or recurrent cases.
plan.EDN: Treat the underlying vasculopathy: glycaemic and blood pressure control. Refer to retina if exudates threaten or involve the fovea.
plan.MH: Find and treat the media opacity itself (cataract surgery, clearing a vitreous haemorrhage). Repeat the fundus exam once the view improves.
plan.MS: No treatment restores the scar. Correct any residual refractive error and consider low-vision aids if central vision is reduced.
plan.MYA: Correct refraction. Screen high myopes yearly for peripheral retinal breaks, staphyloma and myopic choroidal neovascularisation.
plan.ODC: Confirm with intraocular pressure, visual fields and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the nerve fibre layer. Start pressure-lowering treatment if glaucoma is confirmed.
plan.RD: Urgent vitreoretinal referral. Same-day if the macula is still attached. Urgent within days if the macula is already detached.
plan.RT: Treat the underlying disease: panretinal laser or anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) for proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Vitrectomy if traction threatens or involves the macula.
plan.TD: No treatment. Document the appearance to avoid mislabelling it as glaucoma. Check refraction and visual fields once to confirm it is stable.
